newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico slammed for rights record; gov't responds.
newsitem.headline: Mexico slammed for rights record; gov't responds.

text.p: A leading international human rights watchdog group Tuesday issued a scathing report on Mexico, grouping it with the hemisphere's worst human rights offenders.

Torture, arbitrary detentions and "disappearances" are widespread, and the government only appears interested in taking action in cases where members of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) are the victims, the report said.

Human Rights Watch, through its Human Rights Watch/Americas arm, singled out President Ernesto Zedillo for a lack of progress on human rights during his term. Zedillo took office in 1994 pledging respect for the rule of law.

The Foreign Ministry, in a statement late Tuesday, hit back saying the report had been issued to garner publicity ahead of a visit of U.S. President Bill Clinton to Mexico next week. It strongly disputed the report's findings.

"Under the government of President Ernesto Zedillo, there has not been progress," Human Rights Watch investigator Jose Miguel Vivanco told a news conference upon presenting the report. "The levels of impunity are exactly the same as they were five or seven years ago."

While refusing to rank Latin American countries, Human Rights Watch/Americas grouped Mexico in with Cuba, Haiti, Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala as the worst offenders in the hemisphere, Vivanco said.
"Torture is one of the worst evils of Mexico," he said.

Much of the 95-page report focused on the desperately poor southern states of Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero, where guerrilla groups have surfaced, bringing a firm counterinsurgency response from government security forces and alleged paramilitary groups.

There were numerous cases cited in the report of the paramilitary groups, also known as "white guards", who it said secretly do the government's bidding in cracking down on opponents. Local authorities knowingly allow white guards to operate, the report said.
The paramilitary groups were most widely used in Chiapas, attacking leftists and church activists for opposing landed interests, the report said.
In Oaxaca, the report cited several cases of government or paramilitary forces abducting opponents, interrogating them, and setting them free without charges.

In Guerrero, state officials were lambasted for their continuing role in covering up a 1995 massacre that killed 17 peasants. The governor of the state was forced to step down last year because of the scandal.

"The government must place the protection of human rights squarely on its agenda of reform," the report said. "Nowhere is such attention more urgently needed than in Mexico's rural areas, where violent conflict stemming from political and religious differences, counterinsurgency, and disputes over land lead to serious and widespread human rights violations."

In its response, the Foreign Ministry said the report was "partial and unobjective". It also suggested its release had been delayed since March to coincide with Clinton's visit and increase publicity.
